Goldman Sachs cut FMC's price target from $43 to $19, kept its Buy rating, and the stock still lost 61% while the S&P 500 gained 11%.

FMC's Q3 2026 revenue collapsed 78% to $106 million, with an adjusted loss of $4.41 per share against an expected $0.076 profit.

FMC now carries $4.18 billion in debt against negative shareholders' equity, and full-year free cash flow is guided to somewhere between negative $150 million and negative $350 million.

Just released. Our analysts combed the entire stock market and named the ten best stocks to buy right now, and FMC didn't make the cut. Enter your email to see the names that beat FMC. The report is free. Enter your email and see if any of your stocks made the cut.

On October 29, 2025, FMC (NYSE:FMC) reported third-quarter results with the stock at $25.68. By the next day's close it had fallen to $15.53. Then on November 3, Goldman Sachs cut its price target from $43 to $19, a 55.8% reduction, and kept its Buy rating.

Chris Hondros / Getty Images

Since the October 31, 2025 close, FMC has lost 60.9% on a dividend-adjusted basis. Over the same stretch, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) gained 11.2%.

Goldman cut its target by more than half. The cut needed to go much deeper.

FMC Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.
Goldman's Case for Holding On Through the Generic Storm

Goldman's case rested on a split quarter. FMC beat on EBITDA, and adjusted EPS came in at $0.89 against a $0.8548 estimate. Goldman also pointed out the threat directly: generic competition in Latin America had turned out far worse than expected, and the pricing pressure was spreading to FMC's older, off-patent products. Even after cutting its target, the firm still saw value in the shares.

You can follow the logic. The stock had just taken a historic hit, the target still sat above it, and the core problem was named out loud. Goldman read the threat correctly. It underestimated how much damage the threat would do.

title: Bloom Energy Just Joined the S&P 500. Here's What History Says Happens Next.
detail:
Bloom Energy Just Joined the S&P 500. Here's What History Says Happens Next.
Leo Sun, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 30, 2026 at 3:15 PM EDT 4 min read
BE
^GSPC
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Bloom Energy (NYSE: BE), a developer of solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs), has rallied 1,880% over the past two years. Those massive gains -- along with its rising profits -- led to its inclusion in the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) on Sept. 21, 2026.

Could that inclusion pave the way toward even bigger gains for Bloom Energy over the next few years? Let's see what history suggests could happen after it joins the S&P 500.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
How fast is Bloom Energy growing?

Bloom's SOFCs can convert natural gas, biogas, propane, and hydrogen into electricity without any combustion. These clean systems can be deployed quickly, often in less than two months, and bypass traditional utilities that often require years to set up new connections.

The rapid growth of the AI market has driven many big data center operators -- including Oracle, CoreWeave, Nebius, and Equinix -- to deploy Bloom's SOFC systems to expand their cloud infrastructure.

Its new Power Connect System, which reduces its on-site installation time by over 40%, should further accelerate its deployments and widen its moat against other SOFC producers. Brookfield Asset Management, one of the world's largest asset managers, also funds the production and deployment of its systems through a $25 billion partnership.

From 2023 to 2025, Bloom's revenue and adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) grew at CAGRs of 23% and 82%, respectively. At the end of 2025, its backlog hit $20 billion -- nearly ten times the revenue it had generated for the full year.

Why could Bloom's inclusion in the S&P 500 drive it higher?

Bloom's inclusion in the S&P 500 marks a major step in its transformation from a niche green energy play into a high-growth AI infrastructure stock. By achieving the S&P 500's requirement of four consecutive quarters of profitability on a generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) basis, Bloom also counters the bearish notion that its business model is unsustainable.

In the past, many investors likely overlooked Bloom because it wasn't part of a major index. However, its inclusion in the S&P 500 automatically makes it part of any index fund or ETF that passively tracks the index. Therefore, we should see Bloom's trading volume rise significantly as those investors passively purchase its stock. That's why most stocks rise (at least in the short term) after they're added to the S&P 500. For example, Palantir (NASDAQ: PLTR) has rallied nearly 400% since its inclusion in Sept. 2024.

The S&P 500 (^GSPC) is often seen as a benchmark for strong businesses, but that doesn't mean every stock is worth owning. Some companies face significant challenges, whether it's stagnating growth, heavy debt, or disruptive new competitors.

Some large-cap stocks are past their peak, and StockStory is here to help you separate the winners from the laggards. That said, here is one S&P 500 stock that is leading the market forward and two best left off your watchlist.

Two stocks to sell:
Globe Life (GL)

Market cap: $12.33 billion

With roots dating back to 1900 and a rebranding from Torchmark Corporation in 2019, Globe Life (NYSE:GL) is an insurance holding company that offers life insurance, supplemental health insurance, and annuity products through various distribution channels.

Why Is GL Not Exciting?

Sluggish 4.9% annualized growth in net premiums earned over the last five years indicates the firm trailed its insurance peers

Earnings growth over the last two years fell short of the peer group average as its EPS only increased by 12.6% annually

Products and services are facing significant credit quality challenges during this cycle as book value per share has declined by 1.3% annually over the last five years

At $160.17 per share, Globe Life trades at 1.8x forward P/B. To fully understand why you should be careful with GL, check out our full research report (it's free).

U.S. Bancorp (USB)

With roots dating back to 1863 and a presence across 26 states primarily in the Midwest and West, U.S. Bancorp (NYSE:USB) is one of America's largest banks providing lending, deposit services, wealth management, payment processing, and merchant services to individuals and businesses.

Why Are We Hesitant About USB?

Annual net interest income growth of 6.8% over the last five years lagged behind its banking peers as its large revenue base made it difficult to generate incremental demand

Net interest margin of 2.8% reflects its high servicing and capital costs

Performance over the past five years shows its incremental sales were less profitable as its earnings per share were flat

U.S. Bancorp's stock price of $61.02 implies a valuation ratio of 1.5x forward P/B. Read our free research report to see why you should think twice about including USB in your portfolio, it's free.

Booking (BKNG)

From Pandemic Darling to Deliberate Downsizer

Ten years ago, United Parcel Service (NYSE:UPS) was a steady dividend payer trading at $107.76. Then the pandemic turned living rooms into loading docks. Parcel demand surged, pricing firmed, and the stock closed October 2021 at $213.47 before reaching $233.72 in February 2022.

The hangover lasted years. Volumes normalized, a 2023 Teamsters contract raised labor costs, and management chose to shrink its biggest customer by shedding low-margin Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) volume. In 2025, UPS cut about 48,000 positions and closed 93 facilities while chasing premium shipments.

title: Wall Street sell-off deepens as investors question returns on ‘monster AI splurge’
detail:
Wall Street sell-off deepens as investors question returns on ‘monster AI splurge’
Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York City, October 28. - Jeenah Moon/Reuters
Lucy Bayly, John Towfighi, CNN
Fri, October 30, 2026 at 2:59 PM EDT 5 min read
^IXIC
^GSPC
INTC
AMZN
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Wall Street suffered a steep day of losses Friday after the latest tech earnings reignited concerns that massive spending on AI may not deliver the returns that investors expect.

The Nasdaq Composite dropped more than 3.8% and the S&P 500 fell 2.5%, each suffering their worst day since June. The Dow fell 770 points, or roughly 1.5%, its worst day since July.

Just a few weeks ago, the Nasdaq and S&P 500 clinched record highs. But markets were rattled this month as concerns festered about higher interest rates, enormous AI spending and weaker-than-expected earnings and forecasts. The Nasdaq is now down almost 9% from its record high earlier this month, while the S&P 500 is down 3.5%.

Intel plunged more than 30% Friday after issuing weaker guidance for the fourth quarter, citing weakness in the PC market and manufacturing bottlenecks. Amazon shares also dropped, falling 2% following an earnings report that indicated another increase in AI spending.

This comes after shares of Alphabet sank by more than 12% Thursday, wiping half a trillion dollars off the market value of America's fourth-largest company. Investors were concerned about a slowdown in Google's search advertising business and a ramp-up in AI spending. Alphabet shares fell another 1.5% on Friday.

Intel's weaker-than-expected outlook and investors' concerns about the AI boom rattled other semiconductor chipmakers: Nvidia shares dropped 5.6%, while a closely watched index of chipmakers sank 9%.

Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Amazon are collectively spending hundreds of billions of dollars on building data centers. After cheering on anything AI-related, Wall Street is getting more discerning about which companies are spending rationally and seeing tangible returns on investment.

Friday marks the final trading day of a bruising month for AI stocks as investors continue to scrutinize the enormous cost of the AI boom and demand evidence that those investments will eventually translate into profit.

Alphabet's earnings results on Wednesday ignited concerns that Google's core business of search advertising revenue is threatened by consumers using AI chatbots instead of traditional search.

Alphabet's promise of returns from AI "is getting pushed even further down the road," Matt Maley, chief strategist at Miller Tabak + Co, said in a note. "It raises the question as to whether the payout will be as big as they have been promising."

As Big Tech ramps up its spending, investors are getting nervous about its impact to their balance sheets. Google just posted two quarters of negative free cash flow for the first time on record as AI spending accelerates while revenue isn't growing as fast as expected.
